source.name: Google Open Buildings 2023 (confidence 0.80 or higher), with GHSL 2020 where Open Buildings has no coverage

info.content: The map shows one built snapshot, for 2023. It uses Google Open Buildings (2023) polygons with a confidence score of 0.80 or higher. Where that dataset has no coverage — Chad, Mali, Libya, Morocco and Western Morocco — it uses the Global Human Settlement Layer for 2020. A mark means the source recorded a building. It does not say how the building is used. Choosing another year on the timeline still shows this 2023 snapshot, because no other built year is published.

source.name: UMD GLAD tree cover loss via Global Forest Watch

info.content: Tree cover loss from 2001 through the selected year, from University of Maryland GLAD version 1.13, drawn from Global Forest Watch tiles. Loss means the dataset recorded a stand-replacing disturbance, which includes fire and forestry as well as clearing. It is not a measure of deforestation by itself. Version 1.13 adds 2025 and also revises earlier years, so a past year can look different from an older copy of this map. This app does not set a tree-cover density cutoff in the tile request.

source.name: NASA FIRMS active fire detections, counted in 14-day intervals per year

info.content:
Each coloured square is a count of NASA FIRMS detections, not a judgement about why a place burned. The year is split into 14-day windows. A square’s number is how many of those windows contained a detection. The count can reach 27: there are 27 windows, and the last one runs about 13 days into January of the next year. Squares are about 1 km across. Empty squares had no detection in those windows.
  • Light yellow: 1 window
  • Orange: 2 or 3 windows
  • Red: 4 to 8 windows
  • Dark red: 9 or more windows
Colour does not identify agriculture, mining, or a natural fire. Coverage is the Africa export blocks, including some ocean.

source.name: UMD GLAD Global Cropland Expansion in the 21st Century

info.content: Cropland from the UMD GLAD Global Cropland Expansion dataset. The map publishes two snapshots, 2015 and 2019. For any timeline year after 2019, the crops layer still shows 2019. A coloured area means the dataset classed that place as cropland in the snapshot year. It does not show crop type or yield.

Cropland for 2024 from the UMD GLAD annual cropland dataset, clipped to South Africa. This is a different product from the 2015 and 2019 crops snapshots. Orange marks class 1, the dataset's cropland class. The tiles store the class value, and the map applies the colour. Other land and missing data stay clear. It does not show crop type or yield. Tiles run through zoom 12, and closer zoom enlarges them. A timeline year before 2024 does not show this layer.

info.subtitle: Same points every year
info.content: The same dam points are drawn for every year from 2016 through 2022. Moving the timeline does not change them. This catalog does not name the source dataset.

source.name: UMD GLAD tree cover height 2020 via Global Forest Watch

info.content:
Estimated tree canopy height in 2020, in metres. The tiles are already coloured. Pale green is about 3 m, the middle green is about 15 m, and dark green is about 30 m. Canopy taller than 30 m stays dark green. Moving the timeline does not change this layer.
3 m15 m30 m

Source: University of Maryland GLAD dataset umd_tree_cover_height_2020, version v2022, drawn from Global Forest Watch tiles (canopy of at least 3 m). Potapov et al. 2021 describe the canopy-height model. Global Forest Watch lists 2000 and 2020 as the mapped years and links further description to the GLAD 2000–2020 land-cover dataset. Licence CC BY 4.0.

Limits: global coverage at about 30 m. North of 52°N the source calls the map a prototype. The model was calibrated on GEDI relative height at 95% and can overestimate height on slopes, including in New Zealand and Lesotho. In cities it can mix building height with tree height. Canopy below 3 m is not drawn, and heights above 30 m are not separated.
